cost_desc: A hospital DXA scan of the lumbar spine and hip takes a few minutes lying down. Out-of-pocket cost is usually 100–200 yuan, varying by region. Heel ultrasound at a checkup can screen but cannot diagnose.
benefit_desc: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force 2025 recommendation is osteoporosis screening for women aged 65 and older (Grade B). Postmenopausal women under 65 at high fracture risk by assessment should also be screened (Grade B). Evidence for men is insufficient; no recommendation. The evidence review for that guidance pooled 3 randomized trials with 42,009 older European women. Screening meant assessing fracture risk first, measuring bone density in those at high risk, and treating those found high risk. Hip fractures in the screening group were about 17% lower (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.73 to 0.93). In absolute terms, screening avoided 5 hip fractures per 1,000 people. In the UK SCOOP trial of 12,483 women aged 70 to 85, hip fractures in the screening group were about 28% lower (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.89); mortality did not differ. The Chinese Medical Association 2017 guideline recommends DXA for women aged 65 and older and men aged 70 and older, and earlier when osteoporosis risk factors are present. In a 2017–2018 national survey, osteoporosis prevalence among adults over 40 was 20.6% in women and 5.0% in men (China).
plain_terms: Women aged 65 and older, and postmenopausal women with osteoporosis risk factors, should have bone density measured once. When screening starts with fracture-risk assessment and treats those at high risk, hip fractures fall by about 17%. That works out to about 5 fewer hip fractures per 1,000 people screened. Overall mortality did not change.
notes: Controversy: SCOOP's prespecified primary outcome was all osteoporotic fractures; the screening group did not show a clear reduction (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.03)—only hip fractures fell. All three trials used "assess risk, then measure bone density"; none compared bone density testing alone. The evidence review also estimated 11.8% to 24.1% overdiagnosis—people who would never have fractured from this cause in their lifetime. For men, the U.S. says evidence is insufficient; China's guideline sets age 70—follow your doctor. This item is about whether bone can survive a fall; avoiding falls themselves is item 13 (balance and leg strength)—do both. After osteoporosis is found, see item 40 (treat with medication). Primary beneficiaries are you and your parents.

title: If you are diagnosed with osteoporosis, or have fractured from a minor fall, ask a doctor for osteoporosis medication and keep taking it—do not treat calcium supplements as a substitute
cost_desc: Prescription required; use continues for years. Common options include once-weekly oral drugs and once-yearly infusions. Bone density should be rechecked yearly at first, then every 1 to 2 years once stable. The hard part is continuing when you feel fine.
benefit_desc: Fragility fracture means a fracture from minor trauma or everyday activity. The Chinese Medical Association 2017 guideline lists three groups for treatment: prior fragility fracture of spine or hip; bone density T-score −2.5 or lower regardless of prior fracture; or low bone mass plus fragility fracture of wrist, upper arm, or pelvis, or high calculated fracture risk. The guideline states: "There is currently insufficient evidence that calcium supplementation alone can replace other anti-osteoporosis drug therapy." Cochrane's 2025 update on alendronate in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis or prior fracture found hip fractures about 51% lower in the treated group (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.96) and symptomatic vertebral fractures about 55% lower (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.73). The HORIZON trial enrolled 2,127 people mean age 74.5 after hip-fracture surgery; yearly zoledronic acid starting within 90 days post-op, median follow-up 1.9 years. New fractures fell from 13.9% to 8.6% (about 35% relative reduction). Death fell from 13.3% to 9.6% (about 28% relative reduction). The guideline notes about 20% of people die from complications within one year after hip fracture. In the 2017–2018 national survey, only 1.4% of women and 0.3% of men with diagnosed osteoporosis or prior fracture were on medication (China).
plain_terms: If osteoporosis is confirmed, or you have already fractured from a light fall, following a doctor's drug plan cuts hip fractures by about half and symptomatic spine fractures by a bit more than half. In older people who start yearly infusion within 90 days after hip-fracture surgery, new fractures over two years fall by about 35%. Calcium alone cannot replace these drugs.
notes: Controversy: A meta-analysis of 38 trials did not show these drugs lowering overall mortality (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.05). Zoledronic acid alone was also not significant (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.13). The authors concluded these drugs should be used to prevent fractures, not to cut death rates. Cochrane rated those fracture estimates low to moderate certainty. In women without prior fracture and lower risk, alendronate did not clearly reduce hip fractures (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.32). Rare harms such as jaw osteonecrosis and atypical femur fracture may not show up in trials of a few years—keep follow-up visits and do not change dose on your own. Injection versus pills depends on the doctor. How to find osteoporosis is item 39 (bone density testing). Primary beneficiaries are you and your parents.

title: Drill and measure ice thickness before stepping onto outdoor ice; stay off if under 15 cm (6 inches), and avoid river ice and ice fishing holes
cost_desc: The most cost-effective option is to use managed, regulated ice rinks, which incurs no extra outdoor gear cost. If you must venture onto natural outdoor ice, carry an ice auger or chisel to measure thickness, along with a pair of chest-mounted ice rescue picks (safety spikes with handles). These cost under $15–$30. Measuring every few paces as you advance requires some extra time.
benefit_desc: Official meteorological and water safety guidance states that ice must reach 15 cm in thickness before an adult can safely walk or skate on it, and outdoor municipal rinks are generally not cleared for public use below this threshold. Regulated natural rinks typically require a sustained thickness of 15 cm following a full week of continuous sub-zero temperatures (-8°C to 1°C) with low winds before opening. Natural outdoor ice frequently harbors holes drilled by ice anglers, which refreeze poorly and create persistent weak structural points. The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources (DNR) safety guidelines specify that for newly formed, clear ice: stay off if under 4 inches (10 cm); 4 inches is the minimum safe threshold for walking and ice fishing. White ice formed by melted and refrozen snow carries only about half the load-bearing strength of clear ice, requiring twice the thickness. Furthermore, ice thickness varies dramatically across a single water body—it may measure twelve inches in one area and barely one or two inches just a few feet away. Ice over moving water (streams, rivers, beneath bridges, and around culverts) is notoriously hazardous and unpredictable, and shoreline ice is often thinner than open areas. The U.S. National Weather Service sets identical thresholds: under 4 inches is unsafe for walking, fishing, or skating. The Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety (CCOHS), citing Canadian Red Cross recommendations, advises a minimum of 15 cm for small groups walking or skating, and 20 cm for larger group skating gatherings. These benchmarks represent standardized physical safety engineering guidelines rather than empirical epidemiological cohorts.
plain_terms: Official safety standards require ice to be at least 15 cm (6 inches) thick before adults can safely skate on it. Guidelines in the United States and Canada set a baseline of 10 cm (4 inches) for walking or ice fishing, but that applies strictly to clear, newly formed blue ice. White snow ice is only about half as strong and requires double the thickness. On the same body of water, ice can measure a foot thick in one spot and only an inch or two just steps away, so you must measure continuously as you move.
notes: Official safety agencies emphasize that no outdoor natural ice is 100% safe. Meeting minimum thickness is merely a baseline qualification, never a guarantee. The early winter freeze-up and early spring thaw are the most dangerous periods. If you fall through, do not strip off your clothes: trapped air inside winter clothing provides crucial temporary buoyancy. Turn immediately toward the direction you came from, as that ice was solid enough to hold you moments earlier. Place your forearms on the ice shelf, drive your rescue ice picks into the surface, kick your legs horizontally behind you, and pull yourself out. Once out, do not stand immediately—roll horizontally away from the hole until you reach safe ground, then seek warm shelter immediately. If you witness someone else fall through, never run across the ice to grab them: follow emergency rescue protocol (shout for help, call emergency services, extend a pole, or throw a rope from a safe distance), as detailed in Chapter 13, Rule 25. Primary beneficiaries are yourself and children you accompany outdoors.

title: Fit safety guards, wear safety goggles plus a full-face shield before using an angle grinder, grip firmly with both hands, and never mount toothed woodworking saw blades
cost_desc: A pair of impact-rated safety goggles and a full-face shield cost $15–$30. Checking the guard and disc before powering on, and unplugging the tool before changing discs, takes one or two extra minutes. The primary friction is resisting the temptation to remove the protective guard or operate the tool one-handed for convenience.
benefit_desc: Safety directives from the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety (CCOHS) and Workplace Health and Safety Queensland specify clear operating standards: inspect the protective guard and abrasive disc prior to operation; never use discs that are cracked, chipped, or warped. The maximum rated RPM marked on the disc must never be lower than the grinder's spindle speed. Ensure arbor size and disc diameter match manufacturer specifications precisely. Disconnect power before changing discs. Clamp workpieces securely before grinding or cutting. Wear safety glasses or goggles beneath a full-face shield. Maintain a balanced stance with both hands on the tool handles. Never use cutting discs for side-grinding, which causes structural disc failure. Do not put the tool down until the disc has come to a complete stop. Direct sparks and debris away from people and combustible materials. Queensland workplace alerts note that disc edge velocity typically reaches 70 meters per second; fitting a larger 356 mm disc onto a 230 mm tool elevates edge speed beyond 120 m/s, rapidly causing explosive disintegration. In February 2016, an Australian worker using a 230 mm angle grinder was fatally injured when projectile disc fragments penetrated his chest. Formal accident investigations in other jurisdictions record similar fatalities: in 2019, a worker in Harbin fitted a toothed circular saw blade without a guard onto an angle grinder to cut wood; the blade caught his trousers, severed his femoral artery, and caused fatal blood loss before medical aid arrived. In 2024, a renovator in Shenzhen fitted a toothed woodworking saw blade without a guard or auxiliary handle to cut a doorframe; the tool kicked back violently, severing his carotid artery and causing instant death. National and international safety standards (including GB 3883.3 and equivalent ISO/IEC norms) strictly prohibit mounting saw chains, wood-carving blades, or toothed saw blades to handheld grinders. Emergency department injury surveillance in South Korea between 2011 and 2018 tracked 8,697 injuries from high-speed rotating tools, with 4,603 cases caused by grinders: 46.4% sustained hand injuries and 23.0% suffered head/facial trauma. Compared to other rotating tools, angle grinders carried over twice the odds of severe injury (OR 2.07, 95% CI 1.88–2.29). In a hospital study of 36 patients with ocular grinder trauma, 10 sustained permanent post-surgical visual acuity below 0.05 (legal blindness). An orthopedic study of 742 acute forearm and hand injuries in Turkey found angle grinders responsible for 82 cases, of which 44% occurred among retirees doing DIY home repairs. A Japanese trauma series of 15 grinder injuries found 9 were caused by improper attachments such as woodworking blades, resulting in complete finger amputations.
plain_terms: Angle grinders spin at extreme speeds (over 10,000 RPM). If an abrasive disc shatters, fragments fly out at ballistic velocity, and mounting a toothed woodworking blade causes violent, sudden kickbacks. Multiple fatal occupational accidents have documented workers mounting saw blades without guards: one severed a femoral artery, another severed a carotid artery, and neither survived. Safety guards, dual-layer eye/face protection, and a two-handed grip cost very little but prevent fatal injuries.
notes: Grade C is assigned because protocols derive from safety engineering standards and forensic accident investigations rather than randomized controlled trials. Outcomes range from fatal arterial exsanguination to permanent blindness and traumatic limb amputations, exclusively concentrated among grinder operators. Manufacturers explicitly warn against attaching toothed saw blades; woodworking should strictly utilize purpose-built tools such as hand saws, jigsaws, or circular saws with appropriate guards. Ensure loose clothing, jewelry, and long hair are tied back to prevent entanglement. Grinding generates significant airborne particulates and hazardous noise; respiratory and hearing protection standards are detailed in Chapter 19, Rule 10. In the event of acute arterial laceration, immediately apply direct, continuous, heavy manual pressure, as described in Chapter 13, Rule 12. Primary beneficiaries are yourself and bystanders assisting with home renovation.

title: Ask someone who seems emotionally distressed directly "Have you had thoughts of suicide?"—asking will not plant the idea or increase suicidal risk
cost_desc: Zero financial cost. Asking takes seconds, followed by taking time to listen attentively without judgment. The primary difficulty is psychological hesitation, as many people fear that mentioning suicide will introduce the thought into someone's mind.
benefit_desc: In a randomized controlled trial published in JAMA involving 2,342 students across six New York high schools, classrooms were randomly assigned to complete a survey that either included or omitted explicit questions regarding suicidal ideation. Immediately following the survey and at two-day follow-up, emotional distress levels showed no statistically significant difference between groups (P = .66 and P = .41). Two days later, reported suicidal ideation was 4.7% in the surveyed group versus 3.9% in the unasked group—a statistically indistinguishable difference (P = .49). Crucially, students who were already experiencing depressive symptoms experienced significantly lower distress after being asked (P = .01), and individuals with prior suicide attempts showed a significant reduction in subsequent suicidal thoughts (P = .02). A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis evaluating 17 studies pooled 8 comparative trials of asked versus unasked participants: screening or directly inquiring about suicide did not produce any significant increase in immediate or subsequent suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, non-suicidal self-injury, or psychological distress. Across 8 randomized controlled trials evaluated, risk of bias was low or unclear. An earlier 2014 systematic review in Psychological Medicine arrived at identical conclusions: zero identified studies demonstrated an increase in suicidal ideation following direct questioning.
plain_terms: The widespread fear that asking someone about suicide puts the idea in their head is directly refuted by scientific evidence. In randomized trials where high school students were asked detailed questions about suicidal ideation, participants experienced no increase in distress and no rise in suicidal thoughts compared to unasked peers. In fact, students with existing depressive symptoms reported less distress, and those with previous suicide attempts experienced a measurable decrease in suicidal ideation.
notes: Grade B is assigned because while trials conclusively prove that direct inquiry causes no harm, trials cannot ethically measure reductions in completed suicides. Benefit magnitude is rated Low because it reflects surrogate endpoints (ideation frequency rather than absolute mortality counts). Most trial protocols utilized clinical interviews or standardized screening questionnaires rather than informal peer conversations, though clinical guidelines generalize this finding to friends and family. If someone confirms they are having suicidal thoughts, do not leave them unattended: stay with them, connect them immediately to a crisis helpline (such as 988 in the US/Canada or 12356/111 nationally), and remove access to lethal means (medications, sharp objects, chemicals), as outlined in Chapter 1, Rule 25. If they express intent to harm others or have active preparations underway, immediate emergency services or hospital evaluation is necessary, as described in Chapter 8, Rule 15. The interval between acute ideation and action is often mere minutes, as noted in Chapter 1, Rule 32. Primary beneficiaries are family members, partners, friends, and colleagues.

title: If you experience palpitations or an irregular heartbeat, get an ECG; if diagnosed with atrial fibrillation, consult a doctor about anticoagulants to prevent stroke, and do not substitute aspirin
cost_desc: A standard ECG costs just a few dozen yuan (under $10). Warfarin is inexpensive but requires regular blood tests (INR monitoring) to adjust the dosage. Newer direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) do not require routine blood monitoring but are more expensive. The primary challenge is maintaining daily adherence even in the absence of symptoms, and remembering to inform dentists and surgeons that you take anticoagulants before any invasive procedure.
benefit_desc: AFib causes chaotic atrial quivering, leading to blood stasis and thrombus formation. The most common symptoms are palpitations, exertional fatigue, and chest discomfort, though approximately 25% of individuals report no noticeable symptoms. A single-lead ECG recording lasting >=30 seconds or a standard 12-lead ECG lasting >=10 seconds provides definitive diagnosis. A 2007 meta-analysis pooled 29 randomized controlled trials with 28,044 participants: compared to control/placebo, dose-adjusted warfarin reduced stroke by 64% (95% CI 49%–74%), whereas antiplatelet therapy (such as aspirin) reduced stroke by only 22% (95% CI 6%–35%). In direct head-to-head trials, warfarin reduced stroke by an additional 39% compared to antiplatelets. Absolute increase in major extracranial hemorrhage was under 0.3% per year. A Cochrane review evaluating 2,313 individuals with no prior stroke found warfarin lowered all-cause mortality by roughly 30% (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.50–0.94). Four landmark trials totaling 71,683 patients comparing direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) to warfarin demonstrated DOACs further reduced stroke and systemic embolism by 19% (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.73–0.90) and all-cause mortality by 10% (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.85–0.95), with a 52% reduction in intracranial hemorrhage (RR 0.48), despite a 25% increase in gastrointestinal bleeding (RR 1.25). Aspirin cannot replace anticoagulation: in 5,599 patients unsuitable for warfarin, apixaban reduced stroke and systemic embolism by 55% compared to aspirin (HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.32–0.62) with no significant difference in major bleeding (1.4% vs 1.2% per year; HR 1.13, 95% CI 0.74–1.75). In the BAFTA trial of 973 seniors aged >=75, warfarin reduced fatal or disabling stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, or arterial embolism by 52% compared to aspirin (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.28–0.80) with similar extracranial bleeding (1.4% vs 1.6% per year). Chinese 2023 AFib guidelines utilize the CHA2DS2-VASc-60 score (congestive heart failure, hypertension, age >=65 [2 points], diabetes, prior stroke/TIA [2 points], vascular disease, age 60–64, female sex [1 point each]): oral anticoagulation is strongly recommended for males with score >=2 and females with score >=3, and considered for males with score 1 and females with score 2 after weighing bleeding risk. Guidelines explicitly advise against antiplatelet monotherapy for AFib stroke prevention. ACC/AHA 2023 guidelines emphasize anticoagulation decisions depend on thromboembolic risk, regardless of whether AFib is paroxysmal, persistent, or permanent, and bleeding scores should be used to address modifiable bleeding risks rather than inappropriately withhold anticoagulation. National epidemiological surveys (2014–2016) in China of adults aged >=45 found an AFib prevalence of 1.8% (~7.9 million individuals), with awareness at 78.3% in urban areas but only 35.3% in rural areas; among high-risk patients, only 6.0% were receiving anticoagulation. A 2020–2021 nationwide survey found 43.8% of identified AFib cases were newly detected, and among previously diagnosed individuals, only 32.1% were using anticoagulants (19.8% in rural areas).
plain_terms: Atrial fibrillation (AFib) causes the heart's upper chambers to beat chaotically, allowing blood to pool and form clots; if a clot travels to the brain, it triggers a devastating ischemic stroke. Taking doctor-prescribed anticoagulants reduces the risk of stroke by roughly 60% and lowers overall mortality by about 30%. Antiplatelet drugs like aspirin reduce stroke risk by only about 20% and cannot serve as an effective substitute. In national surveys, only a tiny fraction of high-risk patients with AFib were taking anticoagulants.
notes: Controverted in terms of asymptomatic population screening, though anticoagulation following diagnosis is undisputed. Evidence remains insufficient regarding whether asymptomatic individuals should undergo targeted mass screening. The USPSTF (2022) concluded evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of routine screening. The Swedish STROKESTOP trial in 75–76 year-olds found a modest 4% composite reduction in stroke, mortality, and severe bleed after ~7 years, just reaching statistical significance. The Danish LOOP study in 70–90 year-olds with implantable loop recorders detected AFib in 31.8% vs 12.2%, yet saw no significant difference in stroke rates. Chinese 2023 guidelines suggest pulse palpation or opportunistic ECG during routine clinic visits for seniors aged >=65. Thus, individuals with symptoms must be evaluated, and seniors aged >=65 should ask their doctor to check their pulse during visits, but buying dedicated commercial consumer screening monitors is unnecessary. Once on anticoagulants, do not self-administer NSAIDs like ibuprofen without medical supervision, as noted in Chapter 34, Rule 3. Anticoagulants must be taken long-term; never stop them simply because you feel fine, as described in Chapter 16, Rule 1. Hypertension is also a key risk factor, as detailed in Chapter 1, Rule 7. Individuals with AFib do not necessarily need to eliminate coffee, as discussed in Chapter 2, Rule 26. If sudden facial drooping or unilateral limb weakness develops, call emergency services immediately regardless of medication status, as detailed in Chapter 13, Rule 3. Primary beneficiaries are yourself and elderly family members.

title: Adults should screen once for hepatitis C antibodies; if positive, get an RNA test, and if confirmed, complete an 8- to 12-week course of oral antivirals to achieve a cure in over 95% of cases
cost_desc: An anti-HCV antibody blood test costs a few dozen yuan ($5–$15) out of pocket. If positive, a follow-up HCV RNA PCR test determines active viral infection. Confirmed patients obtain prescribed direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) at designated infectious disease clinics; most regimens consist of one tablet daily for 8 to 12 weeks, with medication costs largely covered by national health insurance. The primary challenge is that asymptomatic individuals rarely think to get tested.
benefit_desc: Hepatitis C is a blood-borne viral infection with no preventive vaccine. The World Health Organization (WHO) notes that chronic hepatitis C typically remains asymptomatic for decades, often discovered only after severe liver fibrosis or cirrhosis develops. Antibody positivity reflects past exposure; an HCV RNA test is required to confirm whether active infection is present. Approximately 30% of infected individuals clear the virus spontaneously within 6 months without treatment. WHO states that direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) taken orally for 8 to 12 weeks cure almost all treated patients. An evidence review conducted for the USPSTF pooled 49 treatment trials: sustained virologic response (SVR, defined as undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks post-treatment) exceeded 95% across all genotypes, with serious adverse events occurring in only 1.9% and discontinuation due to adverse effects in 0.4%. Pooling 13 observational cohort studies, achieving SVR was associated with a 60% reduction in all-cause mortality (adjusted HR 0.40, 95% CI 0.28–0.56) and a 71% reduction in hepatocellular carcinoma (adjusted HR 0.29, 95% CI 0.23–0.38 across 20 cohorts). In a French prospective cohort of 9,895 chronic HCV patients tracked for a median of 33.4 months, DAA therapy was associated with a 52% decrease in all-cause mortality (HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.33–0.70) and a 34% reduction in hepatocellular carcinoma (HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.46–0.93) after adjusting for age, fibrosis stage, and alcohol consumption. Among 15,059 U.S. veterans with advanced liver disease treated with DAAs (mean follow-up 1.6 years), mortality was 2.6 deaths per 100 person-years in those achieving SVR versus 12.3 in those who did not, representing a 74% reduction in risk (adjusted HR 0.26, 95% CI 0.22–0.31). The USPSTF (2020) recommends screening all adults aged 18 to 79 (Grade B), with a single lifetime screen sufficient for most people. Chinese 2022 guidelines recommend universal screening for all adults, regular screening for high-risk populations, and immediate RNA testing for all antibody-positive individuals. A 2006 national survey in China found an anti-HCV seroprevalence of 0.43% among ages 1–59; meta-analyses estimated 0.60% in the general population, 48.67% among people who inject drugs, and 6.59% among hemodialysis patients. China's National Healthcare Security Administration reported that before negotiation, full DAA treatment courses often exceeded 50,000 RMB; the 2019 national insurance catalog inclusion lowered prices by over 85%.
plain_terms: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) can silently damage the liver for decades without causing any symptoms; a simple antibody blood test, followed by an RNA test if positive, establishes the diagnosis. For those with active infection, an 8- to 12-week course of oral antivirals clears the virus in over 95% of cases. Achieving viral clearance cuts subsequent overall mortality risk by roughly 60% and liver cancer risk by around 70%. In China, national price negotiations incorporated these therapies into basic health insurance in 2019, slashing medication costs by over 85%.
notes: Controverted by Cochrane (2017), which restricts its evaluation strictly to randomized trials; finding that 138 trials were mostly short-term and assessed surrogate virologic clearance rather than clinical morbidities or long-term mortality, Cochrane asserted that whether SVR translates to reduced mortality has not yet been directly demonstrated in randomized controlled trials. Mortality and liver cancer data presented above originate from extensive prospective longitudinal observational cohorts. No trials directly randomize patients to screening versus no screening. High-risk populations designated for screening include individuals undergoing major surgery, blood transfusion, endoscopy, or hemodialysis; those with unexplained liver enzyme elevations; individuals with a history of intravenous drug use, paid plasma donation, multiple sexual partners, or men who have sex with men; people living with HIV; and regular sexual partners of HCV-infected individuals. In China, many chronic cases trace back to transfusions or plasma donations prior to 1993. Transmission can also occur through unsterilized tattooing, ear piercing, or shared razors and toothbrushes; casual contact (hugging, sharing utensils or cups) does not spread HCV. After successful treatment, antibody tests remain positive for life; RNA testing is required to verify cure or identify re-infection. Successful cure does not confer immunity against re-infection; active injection drug users should undergo annual RNA testing. If discovered during pregnancy, curative treatment is deferred until after delivery and cessation of breastfeeding; strict contraception is required during treatment. Patients with established cirrhosis require ongoing ultrasound surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma even after viral clearance. Avoiding shared needles is detailed in Chapter 1, Rule 30. Hepatitis B requires a separate diagnostic panel, described in Chapter 1, Rule 14. HIV screening is discussed in Chapter 1, Rule 31. Guidelines caution that combining chronic HCV with excessive alcohol markedly accelerates progression to hepatic failure; alcohol limitations are detailed in Chapter 2, Rule 19. Primary beneficiaries are yourself, your spouse, and intimate partners.

title: Ventilate septic tanks, sewer manholes, cesspools, vegetable cellars, and fermentation tanks before entering; if someone collapses inside, never jump in after them—call emergency services immediately
cost_desc: Zero financial cost. Opening all covers and ventilation shafts and waiting upwind takes some extra time. Household septic tanks are safest when emptied by licensed professional service teams with proper equipment. The main difficulty is overcoming the instinct to rush in when a companion or family member collapses.
benefit_desc: A "confined space" refers to enclosed or partially enclosed spaces not designed for continuous human occupancy, including septic tanks, sewage pits, manholes, storage cellars, and industrial vats. An analysis by the Ministry of Emergency Management of China of major confined space accidents since 2013 showed that poisoning and asphyxiation accounted for 96.8% of accidents and 96.9% of fatalities, driven primarily by hydrogen sulfide, carbon monoxide, nitrogen, and carbon dioxide. Accidents involving blind, unequipped rescue attempts accounted for 87.4% of incidents and 86.8% of deaths. The Ministry's 2020 Safety Guidance Manual highlighted that nearly 80% of confined space disasters saw casualties escalate due to impromptu, unprotected rescue attempts, and over 50% of total fatalities were would-be rescuers. In 2018, the State Council Work Safety Committee reported eight separate confined space incidents that initially involved only one worker in distress, but due to successive unequipped rescue entries, resulted in 3 to 4 deaths each. In 2019, during a sewage pit cleaning at a paper mill in Dongguan, three workers collapsed from hydrogen sulfide; six workers entered consecutively to attempt a rescue, resulting in seven deaths. In 2020 at a noodle manufacturing plant in Jiaozuo, one worker fell into a fermentation tank; five coworkers rushed in to assist, resulting in six deaths. The U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) investigated 70 fatal confined space incidents between 1983 and 1993 involving 109 deaths: 39 victims (36%) entered specifically to rescue others, and only 4 of those 39 were trained emergency personnel. A 1986 NIOSH alert estimated that approximately 60% of confined space fatalities were would-be rescuers. Safety manuals explain that while hydrogen sulfide smells like rotten eggs at low levels, high concentrations rapidly cause olfactory paralysis—the human nose completely loses the ability to smell it. Concentrations exceeding 1,000 mg/m³ cause instantaneous "knockdown" and death within seconds. Similarly, extreme carbon dioxide concentrations induce loss of consciousness in seconds. Emergency guidelines strictly mandate: if local personnel lack breathing apparatus and retrieval gear, immediately call 119/120; "under no circumstances should forced entry be attempted." Rescuing an occupant from the outside requires that the entrant was already wearing a full-body harness attached to an external retrieval winch line. Ministerial Order No. 13 mandates that industrial work strictly follow the rule: "ventilate first, test next, enter last." Unventilated subterranean vegetable cellars also pose acute asphyxiation risks because stored root vegetables consume oxygen and release dense carbon dioxide; authorities advise opening all cellar hatches for prolonged natural ventilation, testing air, wearing safety ropes, and maintaining surface observers before entry.
plain_terms: Septic tanks, manholes, cesspools, and sealed vegetable cellars accumulate lethal concentrations of toxic gases (like hydrogen sulfide) and suffer severe oxygen deficiency, knocking an entrant unconscious within seconds. Across official industrial accident registries, a single worker collapses, and coworkers or relatives rush in consecutively to rescue them, only to die alongside them. Official statistics show over half of all confined space fatalities are would-be rescuers. If someone collapses inside, never enter: call emergency dispatch (such as 119 and 120) immediately.
notes: Grade C is assigned because data stem from occupational casualty registries and safety engineering codes rather than clinical intervention trials. Benefit magnitude is rated Moderate: while the event outcome is frequently fatal (often taking multiple lives at once), exposure is concentrated among individuals who access these subterranean structures. Common domestic encounters include cleaning septic or biogas tanks and descending into winter vegetable storage cellars. Never rely on smell to judge atmospheric safety; absence of odor does not mean toxic gas is absent. If assigned by an employer to enter shafts or tanks without mechanical ventilation, gas testing equipment, continuous surface monitoring, or safety harnesses, workers have the statutory right to refuse, as detailed in Chapter 19, Rule 10. If someone collapses inside, shout for help and dial emergency dispatch (119 and 120); external actions are limited to removing covers and using fans or blowers from outside. Once an unconscious victim is extracted to fresh air, check for breathing and initiate chest compressions if breathing is absent, as outlined in Chapter 13, Rule 1. The protocol remains identical whether the victim is a coworker, neighbor, or stranger, adhering to the same safety boundary as Chapter 13, Rule 25 (do not jump into water if you see someone drowning). Carbon monoxide risks from indoor fuel burning are covered in Chapter 1, Rule 3. Primary beneficiaries are yourself (as the prospective rescuer) and coworkers or family members.

title: Adults aged 45 and older living in high-incidence areas for gastric and esophageal cancers, with family history, or tested positive for H. pylori, should undergo screening gastroscopy
cost_desc: A standard diagnostic gastroscopy costs a few hundred yuan ($40–$80); painless gastroscopy with sedation adds several hundred yuan, varying by region. Patients must fast overnight, occupying half a day. Sedated procedures require an accompanying adult. The primary physical discomfort is the passing of the endoscope through the throat during unsedated procedures.
benefit_desc: The 2024 screening protocols issued by the National Health Commission of China define high-risk criteria starting at age 45 with any of the following: (1) residence in high-incidence counties (age-standardized incidence >20 per 100,000 for gastric cancer, or >15 per 100,000 for esophageal cancer); (2) first-degree family history (parents, offspring, siblings) of upper GI cancer; (3) Helicobacter pylori infection (specifically for gastric cancer); (4) lifestyle risks (smoking, heavy alcohol intake, high-salt diet, preserved/pickled foods, or frequent consumption of scalding food/beverages); or (5) personal history of premalignant lesions (atrophic gastritis, gastric ulcers, gastric polyps, Barrett's esophagus, or reflux esophagitis). Screening is recommended between ages 45 and 74, using endoscopy as the primary modality, generally performed every 5 years. The 2022 national guidelines explicitly advise against population screening outside high-risk groups. A population-based cohort study across six high-incidence regions in China tracked ~637,500 individuals aged 40–69: those undergoing a single endoscopic screen had a 57% lower risk of upper GI cancer mortality compared to uninvited controls (unadjusted RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.40–0.47) and a 23% lower cancer incidence (RR 0.77). Screening uptake was 33.53%; on an intention-to-treat basis across the entire invited population, mortality decreased by 31% (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.66–0.72). In a 10-year non-randomized village screening study in a high-incidence esophageal cancer region, cumulative esophageal squamous cell carcinoma mortality was 3.35% in the screened cohort versus 5.05% in the control cohort. In the Korean National Cancer Screening Program, undergoing endoscopy was associated with a 47% reduction in gastric cancer mortality (adjusted OR 0.53, 95% CI 0.51–0.56), whereas upper GI barium series showed no significant benefit (OR 0.98); protection increased with frequent screening. A meta-analysis pooling 10 Asian studies found endoscopic screening was associated with a 40% reduction in gastric cancer mortality (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.49–0.73), without significant change in cancer incidence. In northern China, the ESECC cluster-randomized trial enrolled 33,800 participants aged 45–69 across villages followed for 9 years: esophageal cancer mortality in the screening group was 18% lower (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.53–1.26), which did not reach statistical significance, and incidence was 19% lower (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.60–1.09), also non-significant. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis adjusted for healthy screener bias: among individuals who actually received endoscopic screening, gastric cancer mortality was 48% lower (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.39–0.79), but on an intention-to-screen programmatic basis across all invited individuals, the reduction was non-significant (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.71–1.28).
plain_terms: For individuals aged 45 and older in high-risk categories for gastric or esophageal cancers, undergoing gastroscopy is associated with a roughly 50% lower mortality from these cancers in observational studies. However, people who proactively schedule screenings generally maintain healthier lifestyles, which inflates observational estimates; in rigorous randomized community trials, the reduction in esophageal cancer mortality was approximately 20%, falling within the margin of error. Clinical guidelines advise against routine gastroscopy for average-risk individuals outside high-risk groups.
notes: Controverted in literature. Most evidence demonstrating mortality reduction stems from observational cohorts comparing volunteers who attend screening against non-participants; self-selected participants tend to have higher health consciousness, exaggerating estimated benefits. The 2023 Lancet Regional Health meta-analysis classified study bias risk as moderate to serious. In the cluster-randomized ESECC trial, 9-year mortality differences did not reach statistical significance. The 2022 national guidelines cite potential harms including overdiagnosis, false positives, missed diagnoses, hemorrhage, perforation, cardiopulmonary complications, aspiration pneumonia, and infection. Overdiagnosis refers to detecting indolent early lesions that would never cause symptoms during a lifetime. For those who cannot tolerate standard endoscopy, clinical protocols specify procedures can be performed under sedation or anesthesia. Individuals aged >=45 with positive Helicobacter pylori are categorized as high gastric cancer risk. Eradication of H. pylori is detailed in Chapter 1, Rule 23, but eradication does not eliminate the need for endoscopic screening—both are required. Upper GI barium swallow, serum pepsinogen alone, tumor biomarker panels, and PET-CT scans are not recommended for screening. Commercial tumor marker panels are reviewed in Chapter 6, Rule 7. Those diagnosed with chronic atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, or intraepithelial neoplasia require shorter endoscopic surveillance intervals per gastroenterologist guidance. Residents can inquire with local CDCs or county hospitals regarding whether their area qualifies as high-incidence. Anyone already experiencing alarm symptoms like dysphagia, hematemesis, or melena requires urgent diagnostic medical care rather than screening, as outlined in Chapter 34, Rule 6. Avoiding scalding hot tea is detailed in Chapter 2, Rule 30. Primary beneficiaries are yourself and aging parents.

title: Consume soaked black fungus (wood ear) and silver ear within the same meal without storing overnight, eat fresh wet rice noodles on the day of purchase, and never make fermented cornmeal at home
cost_desc: Zero financial cost. Soak only the quantity of wood ear or silver ear needed for a single meal, and discard any leftovers. Buy only enough fresh wet rice noodles for same-day consumption. The primary difficulty is reluctance to discard surplus soaked fungus, and regional culinary habits of preparing homemade fermented cornmeal dishes (such as suantangzi).
benefit_desc: According to the China National Foodborne Disease Outbreak Surveillance System, between 2010 and 2020, 19 bongkrekic acid poisoning outbreaks were reported, involving 146 illnesses, 139 hospitalizations, and 43 deaths, representing a case-fatality rate of 29.5%. By food category: 9 outbreaks involved homemade fermented corn flour products, causing 33 deaths; 5 outbreaks involved wet rice noodles, causing 7 deaths; and 3 outbreaks involved soaked black fungus, resulting in 5 illnesses and 3 deaths. In 2020 nationwide food poisoning fatalities (143 deaths), bongkrekic acid caused 12 deaths, ranking behind wild poisonous mushrooms (80 deaths) and methanol (14 deaths). Market regulation safety alerts confirm bongkrekic acid is heat-stable and resistant to 100°C boiling and pressure cooking; currently no specific antidote exists. In Guangdong Province, regulatory mandates enacted in 2018 required wet rice noodles to be prepackaged, sealed in small portions, and clearly labeled with expiration dates; post-implementation surveillance showed average annual poisoning cases dropped from 6.25 to 0.5.
plain_terms: Black fungus and tremella (silver ear) soaked for extended periods, improperly stored fresh wet rice noodles, and home-fermented corn flour products can be contaminated by Burkholderia gladioli pathovar cocovenenans, producing bongkrekic acid—a lethal bacterial toxin. Bongkrekic acid cannot be broken down by 100°C boiling or pressure cooking, and there is no known medical antidote. Across nationwide foodborne outbreak surveillance in China over eleven years, nearly 30% of individuals poisoned by bongkrekic acid died.
notes: In October 2020 in Jidong County, Heilongjiang Province, family members consumed homemade fermented cornmeal noodles (suantangzi) for breakfast; all 9 individuals who ate the food died (100% case-fatality). Dried black fungus requires only 1 to 2 hours of cold-water soaking; market guidelines stipulate soaking should never exceed 8 hours. If soaked fungus feels slimy, loses elasticity, gives off a sour or unpleasant odor, or if soaking water becomes turbid, discard the entire batch immediately. If symptoms like vomiting, dizziness, or profound weakness appear after eating, induce vomiting immediately, preserve remaining food samples, and seek urgent hospital emergency care. Anyone who consumed the same food must undergo medical evaluation even if currently asymptomatic. Wild toxic mushrooms are covered in Chapter 1, Rule 5.

title: Quitting smoking, the earlier the better
cost_desc: It costs nothing — in fact, it saves money. A pack-a-day habit costs roughly $3–$4, which you’ll no longer spend after quitting. The hard part is getting through the withdrawal period, which usually lasts a few weeks to several months.
benefit_desc: One U.S. study that tracked participants without assigning them to groups found that current smokers have a life expectancy more than 10 years shorter than those who never smoked. Quitting before age 40 removes about 90% of this excess mortality risk. Quitting between ages 25–34 adds roughly 10 years to life expectancy; between 35–44, about 9 years; and between 45–54, about 6 years (as reported in the original source). Similar Chinese research from the 2010s shows that urban male smokers have a 1.65 times higher death risk than non-smokers (RR 1.65), while rural male smokers have a 1.22 times higher risk. After 10 years of sustained abstinence, this smoking-related risk nearly disappears.
plain_terms: On average, smokers live more than 10 years less than non-smokers. Quitting before age 40 eliminates roughly 90% of the extra death risk caused by continued smoking. The earlier you quit, the more years you gain.
notes: Secondhand smoke is deadly too: in 2004, an estimated 603,000 people worldwide died from exposure to it, accounting for roughly 1% of all global deaths that year. Even if you don’t smoke yourself, you must avoid secondhand smoke, especially to protect children. Specific quitting strategies are outlined in the following sections: Section 3 (smoking cessation medications), Section 4 (setting a quit date), Section 5 (visiting a smoking cessation clinic), and Section 6 (e-cigarettes).

title: Don’t smoke at home or in the car, and don’t let guests smoke indoors
cost_desc: There is no monetary cost and it takes little time. The challenge is simply having the conversation with family members and guests to keep them from smoking indoors.
benefit_desc: In 2004, secondhand smoke caused 603,000 deaths globally — about 1.0% of all deaths worldwide, with children accounting for 28% of those fatalities. Pooled data from 57 studies show that people exposed to secondhand smoke have a 1.28‑fold higher chance of developing hypertension, a 1.39‑fold higher risk of heart disease, a 1.50‑fold higher risk of myocardial infarction, and a 1.36‑fold higher risk of stroke compared to non‑exposed individuals. The risk is greater when exposure occurs at home rather than outside.
plain_terms: Around 600,000 people worldwide die each year from secondhand smoke exposure; nearly 30% of those are children. Long‑term exposure to secondhand smoke raises the risk of hypertension, heart disease, and stroke by roughly 30% compared to non‑exposed individuals. Smoke inhaled at home is even more harmful than smoke encountered outside.
notes: Focus on home environments first, since people spend more time there and pooled research indicates that indoor secondhand smoke is more harmful than outdoor exposure. Children bear 61% of the overall health burden caused by secondhand smoke. For personal smoking cessation, see item 1 in this section.

title: Don’t rely solely on willpower to quit smoking — get medication first: success rates more than double
cost_desc: Nicotine patches and gum are over-the-counter products available at any pharmacy. A full course lasts 8–12 weeks and costs anywhere from a few hundred to over a thousand yuan. Varenicline and bupropion, on the other hand, are prescription-only drugs; you’ll need a prescription from a smoking cessation clinic or a pulmonology department. These costs are roughly offset by the money saved from buying fewer cigarettes during the same period.
benefit_desc: A pooled analysis of 41 randomized trials involving 17,395 participants shows that varenicline increases smoking cessation rates by 2.32 times compared to placebo (RR 2.32, 95% CI 2.15–2.51; high-certainty evidence). Varenicline also outperforms bupropion (RR 1.36, a 36% relative increase) and single-form nicotine replacement therapy (RR 1.25, a 25% relative increase). Across 133 trials with 64,640 participants, nicotine replacement products raise success rates by about 55% versus no medication at all (RR 1.55, 95% CI 1.49–1.61). Using both a patch and a fast-acting form such as gum or lozenges yields a 27% relative improvement over patch-only use (RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.17–1.37; high-certainty evidence from 16 trials with 12,169 participants).
plain_terms: Relying on sheer willpower alone rarely works for most smokers. People taking varenicline are more than twice as likely to succeed compared to those taking a placebo. Those using nicotine replacement products also have a 50% higher success rate than non-medication users. Combining patches with gum or lozenges further boosts success rates by roughly 20%.
notes: In China, these three types of medications are currently available for smoking cessation; only nicotine replacement products are sold over the counter. Common side effects of varenicline include nausea, vivid dreams, and sleep disturbances; anyone with a psychiatric history should discuss this with their doctor. A typical course of nicotine replacement therapy lasts 8–12 weeks — do not abruptly stop use but taper off gradually under medical guidance. While these medications ease withdrawal symptoms during the first few weeks, they do not eliminate cravings triggered by specific situations, so they should be used alongside the other strategies outlined in this chapter: setting a quit date (Section 4) and seeking professional help at a smoking cessation clinic (Section 5).

title: Pick a quit date and stop smoking on that day — don’t taper gradually
cost_desc: No cost at all. Just choose a date on the calendar and let family and coworkers know in advance.
benefit_desc: In the UK, 697 smokers were randomly assigned to two groups. One group quit on a predetermined date; the other cut their cigarette use by 75% during the two weeks before that date. Both groups received nursing support and used nicotine replacement therapy around the quit date. At four weeks, 49.0% (95% CI 43.8–54.2) of the “quit‑on‑date” group remained smoke‑free, versus 39.2% (34.0–44.4) of the “taper‑first” group; the relative risk was 0.80 (0.66–0.93). By six months, 22.0% (18.0–26.6) of the quit‑on‑date group stayed quit, compared with 15.5% (12.0–19.7) of the taper‑first group; the relative risk was 0.71 (0.46–0.91). Even among people who preferred tapering, the quit‑on‑date approach yielded higher success rates at four weeks (52.2% vs. 38.3%).
plain_terms: Many people try to cut back a little each day until they reach zero. Yet after six months, only 15.5% of those who gradually reduced their intake stayed smoke‑free, compared with 22% of people who set a quit date and stopped all at once. So it’s better to pick a date and quit completely on that day.
notes: This is a somewhat controversial topic. Cochrane previously published a review comparing these two methods; it concluded they performed similarly (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.79–1.13, based on 10 trials with 3,760 participants). However, that review was withdrawn in 2019 and is no longer updated. The best current evidence comes from the trial described above, which favors quitting on a set date. Both groups in that trial also used nicotine replacement therapy before the quit date, an approach itself backed by evidence: early use raises success rates by roughly 25% (RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.08–1.44, based on 9 trials with 4,395 participants; moderate‑certainty evidence). Therefore, the recommended strategy is to pick a quit date, start nicotine replacement therapy two weeks beforehand, and then quit all at once on that day.

title: Visit a smoking cessation clinic or call 12320 to find local services
cost_desc: A single clinic visit costs only a few to dozens of yuan. Behavioral support typically involves 4–8 sessions lasting 30–60 minutes each, totaling under 5 hours. Calling the helpline is completely free.
benefit_desc: Across 52 trials involving 19,488 participants, the combination of medication and behavioral support led to a 1.83-fold higher quit rate than standard care or brief advice (RR 1.83, 95% CI 1.68–1.98; high-quality evidence). For the 43 trials conducted in medical settings, this advantage rose to 1.97-fold (95% CI 1.79–2.18). When looking at phone-based support alone: among people who called the helpline themselves, those receiving multiple follow-up calls had a 38% higher quit rate than those who only got informational materials or a single consultation (RR 1.38, 95% CI 1.19–1.61; 14 trials, 32,484 participants). For people who did not call the helpline but received scheduled phone support from researchers, the success rate was 25% higher than those without such support (RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.15–1.35; 65 trials, 41,233 participants). Both findings are supported by evidence of moderate certainty.
plain_terms: Medications and regular follow-up support from professionals are two distinct components that work best together. People who take medication while receiving dedicated follow-up have nearly twice the quit rate of those who only receive brief advice. Phone support also helps: those who proactively call the smoking cessation helpline see their success rate rise by 20–30% compared to others.
notes: How to find local services in China: Search “China Smoking Cessation Platform” on WeChat to access a list of local smoking cessation clinics and helplines, or call 12320 to ask about nearby options. Most of the above trials were conducted overseas, and the intensity of services at local clinics varies widely; these figures should be viewed as general guidelines only. The recommended medications are listed in Section 3 of this chapter (“Smoking cessation medications”).

title: Only consider e‑cigarettes if you’ve already tried quitting; non‑smokers should avoid them
cost_desc: The device plus cartridges cost anywhere from a few dozen to several hundred yuan per month. In China, only tobacco‑flavored e‑cigarettes are legally sold, and only at stores holding a tobacco retail license.
benefit_desc: This up‑to‑date review includes 80 randomized trials involving 29,861 participants. Compared with nicotine replacement therapy, e‑cigarettes raise the quit rate by about 61% (RR 1.61, 95% CI 1.23–2.12; high‑certainty evidence based on 11 trials with 4,114 participants). In absolute terms, that translates to roughly 4 extra quitters per 100 users (range: 1–7). The rate of serious adverse events is similar between groups (risk difference 0.01, 95% CI −0.01–0.02; moderate‑certainty evidence). Compared with behavioral support alone or no support at all, e‑cigarettes improve quit rates by about 75% (RR 1.75, 95% CI 1.39–2.20; low‑certainty evidence).
plain_terms: Switching to nicotine‑containing e‑cigarettes helps roughly 60% more people quit smoking than nicotine patches — this finding is quite reliable. However, e‑cigarettes are not harmless; long‑term safety data remain limited. For people who have never smoked, there is absolutely no benefit to using them.
notes: This topic is controversial. WHO does not recommend e‑cigarettes as a smoking‑cessation tool, citing insufficient long‑term safety data and concerns that they may attract youth to nicotine. The UK, however, includes them in its quit‑smoking services. In China, e‑cigarette sales are not completely banned but are tightly regulated under the “Administrative Measures for E‑Cigarettes.” Only tobacco‑flavored products may be sold, and only at physical stores holding a tobacco retail license; fruit‑flavored e‑cigarettes and refillable devices are prohibited. Sales through any website, online shop, or social‑media platform other than the state‑run e‑cigarette trading platform are illegal, and sales to minors are forbidden. Consequently, fruit‑flavored e‑cigarettes that are still available are sold through illicit channels outside regulatory oversight. This is also how synthetic‑cannabinoid‑laced “high‑effect” e‑cigarettes enter the market; see Section 22, Item 4 (“Do not accept unknown cartridges”). The review examined only legally regulated nicotine‑containing products; unverified e‑liquid mixtures were not included. As a first step, it is advisable to try the medication described in Item 3 of this section, which offers stronger evidence and lower cost.

title: Not drinking sugary drinks — even switching to sugar-free ones doesn’t help
cost_desc: There’s no cost involved, nor does it take any extra time. Switching to plain water or sugar-free tea can even save money. The real challenge is breaking the habit of drinking sweet beverages, including sugar-free ones.
benefit_desc: Two large U.S. studies followed large groups of people without any subgroup categorization; together they included around 118,000 participants and documented 36,000 deaths. Those drinking two or more sugary drinks daily had a 21% higher risk of death compared to those consuming less than one per month (HR 1.21). For those drinking one to two per day, the risk rose by about 14% (HR 1.14). The European EPIC study followed 450,000 people across 10 countries under similar conditions; again no subgroups were defined. Compared to those drinking less than one sugary drink per month, daily consumers of two or more sugary drinks faced an 8% higher risk (HR 1.08, 95% CI 1.01–1.16). Those drinking two or more sugar-free drinks daily had a 26% higher risk (HR 1.26, 95% CI 1.16–1.35). When all types of soft drinks were considered together, the risk increase was about 17% (HR 1.17, 95% CI 1.11–1.22).
plain_terms: People who drink more than two sugary drinks per day have about a 20% higher chance of dying during the same period compared to those who rarely drink them. Those who consume one to two per day still face a roughly 10% higher risk. Switching to sugar-free versions brings no benefit: individuals drinking two or more sugar-free drinks daily actually have a 25% higher risk of death.
notes: There is ongoing debate regarding sugar-free drinks. The association between sugar-free drinks and health outcomes appears even stronger than that of sugary drinks, which likely reflects reverse causality: individuals who are already overweight or have diabetes tend to switch to sugar-free versions. Therefore, we cannot claim sugar-free drinks are more harmful based on this alone. Nevertheless, this evidence clearly shows that the idea “switching to sugar-free drinks solves the problem” lacks any factual support. The safest choice remains plain water or sugar-free tea. Additionally, these studies rely solely on observational tracking rather than controlled trials; people who consume more sugary drinks often lead less healthy lifestyles overall, which may contribute to the observed higher risk figures.

title: Not chewing betel nut
cost_desc: It costs nothing, takes no time, and saves money that would otherwise be spent on betel nut. The hard part is breaking the habit of chewing it.
benefit_desc: Data from 17 Asian studies involving 388,000 participants show that chewing betel nut raises overall mortality risk by about 21% relative to non-chewers (relative risk 1.21, P=0.02). This effect applies to 179,600 of those participants. The risk of diabetes rises by roughly 47% (1.47), while metabolic syndrome risk increases by about 51% (1.51). Betel nut itself is also a known risk factor for oral and esophageal cancer.
plain_terms: People who chew betel nut have roughly a 20% higher chance of dying during the same period compared to non-chewers. Their risk of developing diabetes and metabolic syndrome is nearly 50% higher. Additional risks for oral and esophageal cancer also apply.
notes: The longer and more frequently one chews betel nut, the greater the risk of oral cancer becomes. After quitting, this risk gradually declines over time. Betel nut mixed with tobacco poses an even greater danger.

title: Switch household salt to low‑sodium (potassium‑rich) salt
cost_desc: One bag costs a few yuan more than regular salt. It’s easy to switch when you shop, adding virtually no extra time. The taste stays almost the same.
benefit_desc: A randomized trial conducted in rural China enrolled 20,995 participants — all stroke survivors or adults aged 60+ with hypertension — and followed them for 4.74 years. Those using low‑sodium salt had a 12% lower risk of death (RR 0.88), a 14% lower risk of stroke (RR 0.86), and a 13% lower risk of major cardiovascular events (RR 0.87) compared with the regular‑salt group. No statistically significant difference emerged between the groups regarding episodes of excessively high blood potassium levels.
plain_terms: For people who have had a stroke or are over 60 with hypertension, switching to low‑sodium salt can lower their chance of dying within five years by about 12% and the risk of another stroke by roughly 14%.
notes: This finding is somewhat controversial. The PURE study only recorded long‑term outcomes without random assignment; it reported that individuals excreting less than 3 g of sodium per day faced a roughly 27% higher risk of death or cardiovascular events, while those excreting more than 7 g per day faced a 15% higher risk. According to PURE, both very low and very high sodium intake are detrimental, with moderate intake being optimal. However, the Chinese rural trial only partially replaced regular salt with low‑sodium salt, so sodium levels did not drop to the extremes examined in PURE. Moreover, the trial involved only high‑risk elderly participants; younger, healthier individuals would likely gain far less benefit. People with impaired kidney function or those taking potassium‑sparing medications should consult a physician before making this switch.

title: Brush teeth thoroughly, clean between teeth daily, and see a dentist if you have missing teeth
cost_desc: Dental floss or interdental brushes cost just a few dozen yuan per year, while professional cleanings run about 100–200 yuan each. It takes only two to three extra minutes per day. The real challenge is making flossing a daily habit.
benefit_desc: A Japanese study followed 9,676 participants for six years. Those who used interdental cleaning tools saw their mortality risk drop by about 11% (hazard ratio 0.89). Those who used tongue cleaners saw a 23% reduction (HR 0.77). When multiple studies of community-dwelling seniors are combined, people with no natural teeth have roughly 1.87 times the risk of death (95% CI 1.35–2.59). Those with fewer than 20 natural teeth face about 2.04 times the risk (95% CI 1.67–2.49).
plain_terms: People who clean between their teeth daily have roughly a 10% lower chance of dying over the same period. For elderly individuals with no natural teeth, the risk of death is about 90% higher. Those with fewer than 20 natural teeth face roughly double the risk. Having missing teeth evaluated by a dentist protects periodontal health and eating function.
notes: This topic remains debated. These studies are purely observational; individuals with poor dental health often also have poorer overall health and lower socioeconomic status. It is unclear whether poor dental health directly drives systemic disease or reflects general decline; getting dental implants or dentures has not been directly tested in trials for mortality reduction. Regardless, the cost of proper oral hygiene is very low, and missing teeth directly impair nutritional intake and masticatory function.

title: Walking 7,000–8,000 steps per day, or accumulating 150–300 minutes of brisk walking each week
cost_desc: It costs nothing. In terms of steps, walking 60–90 minutes daily can easily be split into short bouts during commutes or errands. In terms of time, it requires just 20–45 minutes per day. The real challenge is maintaining this habit over the long term.
benefit_desc: Fifteen studies tracking large groups of people were combined for analysis without subgrouping. These studies included 47,471 participants and 3,013 deaths. When grouped by daily step counts, the lowest group had a median of 3,553 steps/day; the next three groups had medians of 5,801, 7,842, and 10,901 steps/day. Their mortality risks were roughly 40%, 45%, and 53% lower than the lowest group (HR 0.60, 0.55, 0.47 respectively). For those over 60, benefits plateau after reaching 6,000–8,000 steps/day; for younger adults, the plateau appears at 8,000–10,000 steps/day. Another analysis found benefits begin at around 3,867 steps/day; each additional 1,000 steps/day reduces mortality risk by roughly 15%. When measured by exercise time, individuals meeting 1–2 times the recommended weekly activity level (7.5–15 MET·h/week, equivalent to 150–300 minutes of brisk walking) had a mortality risk about 31% lower than inactive people (HR 0.69). Those below this threshold still saw a 20% reduction (HR 0.80), while those exceeding it 3–5 times saw a maximum reduction of 39% (HR 0.61). Further increases bring no additional benefit, though they pose no harm (HR 0.69 at >10 times the threshold). A final study using accelerometers showed that the top quarter of participants in terms of moderate-to-vigorous activity had a mortality risk roughly 48% lower than the bottom quarter (HR 0.52). Accelerometers are wearable devices that measure actual physical activity levels.
plain_terms: People who walk roughly 7,800 steps daily have a mortality risk roughly 45% lower than those walking only 3,500 steps. The same pattern holds when measured by time: those who engage in 150–300 minutes of brisk walking weekly face about 30% lower risk than inactive individuals. Beyond a certain threshold, further increases bring little extra benefit; for people over 60, 6,000–8,000 steps per day is sufficient. Meeting either step target is enough.
notes: Step counts and exercise time describe the same behavior; meeting either target suffices. The greatest benefit is seen when increasing daily steps from 4,000 to 7,000; there is no need to reach 10,000 steps. It is important to note that these studies merely track activity levels; the least active participants often include those already ill or frail, which can inflate observed risk differences. Studies relying on accelerometer measurements tend to involve shorter follow-ups and older populations, so their reported benefits may be somewhat overestimated. Nevertheless, the overall trend of greater activity leading to better outcomes remains clear.

title: Screen blood lipids regularly in adulthood (every 2 to 5 years before age 40, annually from age 40); take prescribed medication consistently for hypertension and dyslipidemia, never stopping on your own
cost_desc: Generic hypertension drugs and statins cost only a few to several dozen yuan per month. They are taken once daily, requiring minimal time. The real challenge is sticking to them long-term rather than stopping once you feel better. Checking blood lipids requires a blood draw; adults aged 65 and older have an annual free health checkup including lipid screening (see Chapter 6, Rule 18).
benefit_desc: Pooled data from multiple randomized controlled trials show that a 10 mmHg reduction in systolic blood pressure lowers mortality by about 13% (RR 0.87) and major cardiovascular events by roughly 20% (RR 0.80). Stroke risk drops by around 27% (RR 0.73), while heart failure risk decreases by about 28% (RR 0.72). Statins also reduce LDL cholesterol; each 1.0 mmol/L drop lowers mortality by roughly 10% (RR 0.90) and major vascular events by about 22% (RR 0.78). Observational studies further indicate that patients who adhere to prescribed treatment regimens (>=80% compliance) enjoy significantly lower mortality rates: statin adherence reduces risk by about 45% (RR 0.55), while adherence to antihypertensive therapy lowers risk by roughly 29% (RR 0.71). Official Chinese lipid guidelines and the Healthy China Action recommend regular lipid profiling: every 2 to 5 years for adults aged 20 to 39, annually for adults aged 40 and older, and every 6 months for high-risk individuals.
plain_terms: For every 10 mmHg drop in systolic blood pressure, mortality decreases by roughly 13%, while stroke risk drops by about 27%. Each 1.0 mmol/L reduction in LDL cholesterol achieved by statins lowers mortality by roughly 10%. Those who take their medication as directed have a 30% to 45% lower risk of death compared to those who frequently miss doses. Adults should check blood lipids every 2 to 5 years before age 40, and annually starting at age 40.
notes: Only individuals deemed by doctors to need medication should follow this advice; healthy people do not require medication. The figures regarding consistent medication use stem from observational data; those who stick to treatment tend to be more disciplined overall, which may inflate perceived benefits. The mortality reductions linked to blood pressure control and statins are firmly supported by randomized trials. Routine lipid screening catches silent hyperlipidemia early before coronary artery disease or stroke occurs. Primary beneficiaries are yourself and your parents.

title: Getting about 7 hours of sleep each night with a consistent schedule
cost_desc: No cost involved. You simply need to allocate time for sleep — most people achieve this by cutting back on phone usage. The real challenge is maintaining a fixed bedtime and wake‑time.
benefit_desc: A pooled analysis of 16 longitudinal studies — involving 1.38 million participants and 113 000 deaths — shows that short sleepers face a 12% higher risk of death (RR 1.12), while long sleepers face a 30% higher risk (RR 1.30). When sleep duration is grouped into categories, the 7‑hour bracket shows the lowest risk; each additional hour beyond 7 raises risk by about 13% (RR 1.13), and each hour less than 7 raises it by roughly 6% (RR 1.06). In the UK Biobank, wrist‑watch data from ~61 000 participants were used to rank them into five groups based on schedule regularity; the four more regular groups had a 20%–48% lower mortality risk than the least regular group. Another UK Biobank study tracked 51 562 individuals for new cardiovascular events; those with a social jet‑lag of 2 hours or more faced a 30% higher risk (HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.11–1.54), and this link persisted even among people getting a normal amount of sleep.
plain_terms: People who regularly get less than 7 hours of sleep have roughly a 10% higher chance of dying over time. The more irregular their schedule, the greater the risk. Those with the most regular sleep patterns enjoy a 20%–50% lower mortality risk compared to those with the least regular patterns. In other words, how consistent your sleep schedule is matters more than the total number of hours you sleep.
notes: The main issues to address are insufficient sleep and irregular schedules; there’s no need to deliberately shorten sleep time. The elevated risk seen in long sleepers is likely reversed causality — depression, chronic illness, and sleep apnea tend to cause longer sleep durations. Currently, only two longitudinal studies support the benefit of a regular schedule; both are observational and ungrouped, so they constitute B‑grade evidence on their own. For ways to recover after staying up late, see Section 38 (recovering sleep after a late night). 〔113000〕 〔61000〕 〔51562〕 〔3853〕

title: Playing racket sports three times a week for 45 minutes each session
cost_desc: The cost of court fees is typically a few dozen yuan per session. This amounts to roughly 2 hours of activity per week. The main challenge is arranging enough participants and securing a court, plus maintaining consistency week after week.
benefit_desc: A UK-based study tracking 80,300 participants compared those who engaged in racket sports with those who did not. The former group had a 47% lower overall mortality risk (hazard ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.40–0.69). Their risk of cardiovascular death was 56% lower (0.44, 95% CI 0.24–0.83). Racket sports here include tennis, badminton, and table tennis. For swimmers, these figures were 0.72 and 0.59 respectively; for aerobic exercise enthusiasts they were 0.73 and 0.64, and for cyclists 0.85. No statistically significant differences were found between runners and soccer players.
plain_terms: People who regularly play tennis, badminton, or table tennis have about half the risk of dying during the same period compared to non-players. Their risk of dying from cardiovascular causes is roughly 56% lower. Swimmers enjoy a similar benefit, with a 28% lower risk. No significant difference was observed between runners and soccer players in this data set.
notes: This finding remains somewhat controversial. Such studies are purely observational in nature. People who play racket sports tend to be healthier overall and enjoy more social interaction. The lack of difference seen among runners suggests that individual characteristics may play a role in how exercise impacts health outcomes. This does not mean running offers no benefits; a separate entry in this section examines overall exercise volume instead.

title: Accumulating brief bouts of strenuous activity like stair climbing or brisk walking to total 4–5 minutes per day
cost_desc: There is no cost involved, and no extra time needs to be set aside for exercise. The main challenge is remembering to climb stairs or walk briskly instead of taking shortcuts.
benefit_desc: A study conducted by the UK Biobank involved 25,200 participants who did not engage in regular exercise. After an average follow-up period of 6.9 years, 852 participants passed away. Those who completed three 1–2 minute bouts of strenuous activity daily saw their overall mortality risk and risk of cancer-related death drop by 38%–40%. Their risk of cardiovascular death fell by 48%–49%. Even those who accumulated just 4.4 minutes of such activity per day experienced a 26%–30% reduction in overall mortality and cancer death risk, as well as a 32%–34% drop in cardiovascular death risk.
plain_terms: For individuals who do not exercise regularly, performing just three 1–2 minute bouts of strenuous activity each day can reduce their overall risk of death by roughly 40% compared to those who do none at all. Their risk of dying from cardiovascular causes also drops by nearly half. Such strenuous activities include stair climbing and brisk walking.
notes: This finding is somewhat controversial. The study relied on wearable devices to accurately measure physical activity levels, which is more reliable than self-reported survey data. However, it remains an observational study without any randomized controlled trials, and the follow-up period was only 6.9 years. These results apply only to people who do not exercise regularly, and may not hold true for those who already maintain a regular exercise routine.

title: 30–60 minutes of strength training per week
cost_desc: Doing bodyweight squats and push-ups costs nothing. Aim for 1–2 sessions per week, each lasting 20–30 minutes. The real challenge is fitting this into your weekly schedule.
benefit_desc: When multiple observational studies are pooled together (without subgroup analysis), individuals who perform strength training show a 10%–17% reduction in mortality risk relative to non‑trainers. This benefit peaks at roughly 30–60 minutes of weekly training, delivering a 10%–20% risk drop; more training does not further improve outcomes. Those who also do aerobic exercise enjoy an even lower mortality risk than those who do neither type of exercise.
plain_terms: People who engage in 30–60 minutes of strength training each week have a 10–20% lower risk of dying during that period compared to those who don’t train at all. Training beyond this amount won’t bring any extra benefit. Combining strength training with aerobic exercise yields the best results.
notes: These studies rely on follow‑up tracking, with participants self‑reporting their activity levels. The evidence supporting the notion that “excessive training can be detrimental” is quite weak, so there’s no need to cap training volume for that reason. For older adults, strength training also helps prevent falls and preserve muscle mass; those benefits are discussed in Section 1.

title: Don’t sit for too long at a time — get up and move every now and then
cost_desc: It costs nothing; getting up a few times doesn’t take much time at all. The hard part is that once you sit down, you tend to lose track of time, so you need a reminder.
benefit_desc: One U.S. observational study used accelerometers to measure activity levels without grouping participants. It divided people into four groups based on their total daily sitting time. Those in the group with the most daily sitting time had a 2.63 times higher risk of death than those in the group with the least (HR 2.63). The study also split participants into four groups based on the longest continuous sitting period; those in the group with the longest continuous sitting time had a 1.96 times higher risk than those in the group with the shortest continuous sitting time (HR 1.96). This shows that both total daily sitting time and the length of each continuous sitting period are independently linked to mortality risk. Another meta-analysis of millions of participants also used observational data without grouping. It found that people who sat for over 8 hours a day and did little to no exercise had a 1.59 times higher risk of death compared to those who sat for less than 4 hours a day and were the most active. For the most active group, even if they sat for over 8 hours a day, their risk ratio was only 1.04 — no statistically significant difference was observed.
plain_terms: People who sit the longest have a 2.6 times higher chance of dying during the same period compared to those who sit the least. Sitting continuously for long stretches adds extra risk on top of that. However, if you get 60–75 minutes of moderate-intensity activity each day, this extra risk from prolonged sitting is largely offset.
notes: The reliable conclusion here is that how much you move matters more than how long you sit; when you get enough exercise, the extra risk from prolonged sitting largely disappears. It’s worth noting that these studies are purely observational, so many of the people who sit the most already have underlying health issues — the “2.63 times higher risk” partly reflects this pre-existing health condition. Additionally, the same meta-analysis found that watching TV for over 3 hours a day increases risk across all activity levels; for the most active group, this risk threshold only rises to 5 hours a day.

title: Eat less processed meat (ham, bacon, sausages, luncheon meat)
cost_desc: It costs nothing — in fact, it saves money — and doesn’t take extra time. The hard part is simply eating less of a food you really enjoy.
benefit_desc: When multiple long‑term studies are pooled together (without separating participants into groups), the group eating the most processed meat faces about a 23% higher risk of death (RR 1.23) than the group eating the least.
